WENTWORTH HEROIN WAR

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Drugs, guns and drive-by shootings are at the centre of a turf war claiming lives of rival gang members and innocent bystanders in Wentworth, in Durban South.

Unique Selling Point:
WHAT WE HAVE
** CCTV FOOTAGE OF 2021 HIT
** UNDERCOVER FOOTAGE
** LAB TESTS
** INSIDER

This has all the elements of an investigative - powerful layers, strong interviews and sexy elements that viewers will love. I believe this will hold for 12.

Summary:
We covered the rise of codeine addiction in the Wentworth community back in 2018. Now it’s heroin capsules – package as pills, packing a deadly punch with dealers undercutting each other and taking out the opposition.

Rival gangs shoot first and don’t ask questions.

We delve into the driving forces and unpack the disturbing reality of life in Wentworth - a community crippled by poverty and drug addiction.

Further information:
The gangs are engaged in a ‘race to the bottom’ price war, with capsules selling for as low as R10. These prices brought more customers, but also more violence - the guys in Wentworth are killing each other over price – as simple as that.

We go undercover and show how easy it is to buy drugs and take it one step further by testing the contents of these new capsules hitting the streets and speak to a community gripped by fear.

UNDERCOVER ELEMENT
- We managed to do 4 buys in just 45 minutes – every time a different price.
** HIDDEN CAMERA FOOTAGE & DEALER INTERACTIONS

THE SCIENCE
We have the samples analysed to determine what the actual contents are and speak to the pharmacology team that unpacked this drug that is unique to KZN.

WHY HEROINE CAPSULES?
Capping heroin makes for more time-efficient packaging and provides for easier and more precise dose allocation, with the capping machine ensuring that the same measure of heroin is inserted in every capsule, which makes counting of doses and distribution to dealers easier.

Suppliers or wholesalers can service dealers who have different size customer bases, effectively removing layers of middlemen from the distribution pyramid. Capping machines means that fewer people are involved in heroin processing and the potential for information leaks is reduced, making production more secure.


BRAND AWARENESS – EVEN WHEN IT COMES TO DRUGS
Capsules may make it easier for drug kingpins to stash drugs with associates and keep track of merchandise. The colour and markings of the capsules is also significant. A host of different coloured heroin capsules with a variety of markings and logos have been seized in Durban busts.

An identifiable capsule brand allows networks to build up a kind of ‘brand recognition’. This helps networks reinforce control over drug sales on their turf and become associated with the quality of the heroin –an important distinguishing quality in an expanding market characterized by fierce competition.

SAPS members said that some drug lords sourced heroin from the same wholesalers at times, but increasingly they sought to differentiate themselves from rivals.

METRO CAPSULES A TOP SELLER
The case of the ‘Metro’ capsule – so called because the blue and white capsules matched Durban Metro Police vans – highlights the importance of product brand, quality and consistency in capturing, retaining and growing a market. ‘The addicts went wild for the blue and white cap when it first hit the streets,’ according to a SAPS officer. SAPS members said the capsules were sought after until either the producer’s quality dropped or poorer-quality copies emerged. The SAPS officer said police noticed a marked response to the quality of the heroin capsules. ‘If the users don’t get a good hit they will drop a dealer.’

TURF WAR
There are so many little gangs operating with a number of runners on the streets. The area is a just a few blocks and every street is just about a different dealer’s turf. Even with our undercover we could see that the price discrepancies would fuel a turf war.

THE CASUALTIES
• May 17, 2021 A DRIVE-BY shooting outside a block of flats in Wentworth has claimed the life of a bystander.Police reports said a group of people were sitting outside block 25 flats on Burgess Road at 10.45pm on Friday night socialising, when a silver-grey Toyota Etios stopped. The front left passenger window opened and the passenger, who cannot be identified, fired several shots with a handgun at the group.Police said about 20 rounds could have been fired. The Etios then sped off. It is alleged Rabia Elouise was standing near the gate at the entrance to the flats.Three people had bullet wounds on their legs. Two are recovering in hospital. The concrete palisade fencing was pockmarked with bullet holes at the entrance to the flats.
• Days later, yet another shooting in Wentworth, following an incident that left a man wounded. The man was recovering in hospital after being shot three times in a drive-by shooting in Wentworth, south of Durban, on Monday.The incident happened in Woodville Road, where rival drug gangs have been killing each other for the past year.
• 13 JUNE 2021: Brian Captuiex, 55, of Reiger Road, was in his vehicle outside his home when he was shot. Captuiex was talking to friends when a vehicle stopped nearby and he was shot in the chest. Police claimed it could have been a case of mistaken identity and that Captuiex was perhaps not the intended target.
• the second incident, a 15-year-old boy was shot in Silvertree Road, less than 2km from the first shooting. he boy was shot by a known suspect at the corner of Lawler and Tifflin roads. He sustained a gunshot wound on the left side of the abdomen. He was rushed to hospital for medical attention – but died.
• 02 JULY 2021 – a young man was stabbed to death in an argument about turf.

WE HAVE FOOTAGE OF A HIT THAT KICK STARTED THESE RETALIATION SHOOTINGS
JANUARY 2021

A top lieutenant in Cartel gang was assassinated in January 2021. Bradley Davids, aka Gooch, was shot and killed by two gun men who pulled up behind him moments after he got into his car on Stableford Road in the Bluff. His murder came on the same night that rival drug gangs shot at each other in Wentworth as frightened residents cowered in the homes behind drawn curtains.

According to highly placed police sources, Davids was a senior member of the Cartel gang, whose leader, Simone aka “Moni” Jasmin was killled in a hit in October last year.
He is said to have run the Woodville and Woodstock Road drug corners of the gang.

According to police and Wentworth residents his murder is a result of the power vaccum left in the wake of Jasmin’s killing and the fact that several other high ranking members of the gang are in prison awaiting trial on murder charges.
Wentworth residents, angered by random shootings and drug dealings in the area, confronted alleged drug runners in their homes.
A BROKEN COMMUNITY
“Innocent lives are being taken. If we don't do something today, the community will not belong to us tomorrow. It will belong to the drug lords,” said a pastor. “There is power in numbers. Our youths are the ones endangering their lives and our lives. We cannot keep quiet any longer. The sale of drugs is so bad that we are getting outsiders coming to our area and killing innocent people.”
• Another resident said parents should be informed if their children were selling drugs in the community. “One boy sells drugs outside my house. I told him to go away. His response was that he could not sell in front of his mother’s house. So they are scared to sell in front of their parents’ homes but they want to endanger us.
• A fellow resident said she was threatened by a group of young boys for speaking out about drugs. She said last week, she overheard two drug runners arguing about a spot in front of her house. They each claimed the area as their territory. “It’s my house. They live far away. They were arguing about whose spot it was for selling. When I went out to see what was happening, the one guy pulled out his gun and started wiping it. How do you have a gun with you so freely?”
• Hector Henry, 86, a community activist, said people should take a stand and go to the eThekwini Municipality to ask for more security in the area.“Take the bull by the horns and stand firm. Last year, a person was shot and that person’s mother is still waiting for the police to come over and take statements. We need to call on law enforcement to make their presence known and to help us get rid of all the illegal nonsense going on here.”
Community activist Desmond D’Sa also blamed the court, which he described as having “revolving doors”.
“The shooters and dealers go in and come out again within a week. We need to approach the National Prosecuting Authority. This drug den operates with impunity in full view of the public.”
D’Sa said that the recently established Anti-Gang Unit should be pulled away from their other responsibilities and moved into Wentworth as it was a hot spot.
“They need to get to the bottom of who the kingpins are. Those that are known, who don’t live in the community but recruit the youngsters to do their dirty work. People are living in fear and it is time that these killings come to an end,” he said.
NO FAITH IN POLICE
TRACY WILLIAMS from the a non-profit organisation working with the community – they say there is little trust in the police and Wentworth has been forsaken – she explains that the community is not co-operative because they fear for their lives. They are reluctant to give information to the police. Witnesses are threatened. Lives are destroyed. Youngsters on drugs are irresponsible. Many youngsters have lost their lives, some boys want to make a name for themselves. They do not fear death. The people behind it do not have a conscience.


INTERVIEWS
- UNDERCOVER FOOTAGE
- PROF THAVI GOVENDER, UKZN PHARMACOLOGY DEPARTMENT – ON THE RESULTS, he has done research into street heroin and other street drugs in Durban.
- DR MONIQUE MARKS - Initially trained as a social worker, she has a doctorate in Sociology from the University of Natal, and writes predominantly in the field of criminology – she will talk about the rise capsules and the turf war.
- COP INSIDER – WHY ISN’T IT WORKING
- TRACY WILLIAMS – THE COMMUNITY VOICE // MAYBE ALSO DES D’SA – TRYING FOR A FAMILY MEMBER – BUT MOST IN DENIAL ABOUT THE VICTIM’s INVOLVEMENT IN THE DRUG WORLD
- SAPS – HARD INTERVIEW



Extra Budget Items:
** Investigative Rate Potential as discussed in frying session with regards to the undercover elements and risks attached, the additional layer of the lab testing and the cop insider that will speak out about the ineffectiveness of the current anti-gang unit. I've also spent quite some time on this story researching it and finding the right ways to do the undercover.

Script:


STUDIO INTRO: A trend for capsulised heroin has been sweeping Durban in recent years — with more efficient packaging, production and distribution, Durban has been ravaged by the consequences of addiction, and criminal competition. We went undercover in Wentworth to show you just how blantant the drug trade has become.

STRUCTURE
VO: Buying drugs in Wentworth in the south of Durban is as common as buying bread and milk.

In broad daylight. On every second street corner, there is a runner – brazenly dealing drugs.

SEQUENCE OF DEALS

INSIDER: The drug trade is alive and it’s thriving. It's not coming from yesterday. It's been years And obviously, what goes with drugs is shootings and driveby’s.

LINK: RIVAL GANGS SHOOT FIRST AND ASK QUESTIONS LATER. THE COMMUNITY IS CRIPPLED BY DRUG ABUSE AND GRIPPED BY FEAR IN AN AREA WHERE LIFE CHEAP AND JUSTICE IS SEEMINGLY HARD TO FIND

VO: Criminologist, Professor Monique Marks, has done extensive research in the field of drug use.

MONIQUE: Where drug use is very active, there will be gangs involved. And because it's such a lucrative business, // there will be turf wars around who has a monopoly over that business.

VO: In the last year, at least 15 people have been killed in drive-by shootings, stabbings and murders – some innocent by-standers caught in crossfire, while others were linked to the drug underworld.

In January this year, an alleged top lieutenant in one of the notorious Wentworth Gangs was assassinated. Watch this CCTV footage as Bradley Davids, aka Gooch, was shot and killed by three gunmen. The shooters pulled up behind him and opened fire.

A so-called Wentworth gangster agreed to speak to us on condition of anonymity. He has been in the inner circles for more than a decade and has even served time for committing a hit.

MAC: These shootings, though, you know, I mean, it's one thing that people are taking drugs, but it's tend to like violence.
GANGSTER: They want to take over, they want to be the Godfather’s of Wentworht. And it's not going to happen that way. A lot of life is being dropped because people are fighting

NOLENE: // All Fighting for the small place in Wentworth and turning our beautiful community into a horrible community.

VO: Wentworth residents, like Nolene Ogle are angered by the senseless random shootings, fuelled by a growing drug trade.

MAC: And how old would you say these kids are that are pulling the trigger ?
NOLENE: They're like from 14 and up
MAC: 14?
NOLENE: 14 years old and up
MAC: already carrying guns
NOLENE: -already carrying guns. M7
MAC: And how often do these shootings happen?
NOLENE: It happens like almost every day of the week

VO: This Durban cop works drug related cases - he says what we’re seeing in Wentworth is often revenge killings.

INSIDER: these guys are ruthless, they they're not trained marksmen or shooters, there’s no specific target that's aimed

VO: One of the most recent innocent victims was 12 year old, Virdene Stanley. She is currently in hospital recovering from a head wound, having lost her right eye completely.

We spoke to her mom, Virasha Ali – they were at home watching television when the gunmen opened fire.

VIRASHA: These are all from the same shooting, bullet hole there, bullet hole there – as they came shot there
MAC: Where was your daughter, she was sitting where ?
VIRASHA: her dad was sitting there ad she was sitting next to her dad// as we heard the gun shots we all took cover,
MAC: where was she shot
VIRASHA: The bullet went through here and exited here//
MAC: But how does this make you feel as a mom?
VIRASHA: Because, I mean, it was so heart breaking, //. It's not something easy. My family is traumatized and i’m traumatized.

VO: It’s alleged that the attack was in retaliation to the killing of a member of a rival gang in the street just below. We were there on the day of the funeral, the tension was palpable.

LINK: A number of smaller gangs operate in the area with runners on the streets. It’s a few blocks, where just about every street is a different dealer’s turf. They undercut and fight for territory day in and day out.

GANGSTER: Wentworth people they’re their own boss, you can’t just come and take over another man’s turf, you come with bullets, you get of bullets.

VO: One of the main products is Heroin Capsules. Packaged to look like pills, the contents are not pharmaceutical in any way.

Interested to test the market, we followed undercover operatives. Within 45 minutes, 4 buys were made in a 2km radius.

While the runners hustle for cash, they know what they’re doing is illegal.


RUNNER: The police they watch here
OPERATIVE: Where’s the R10 change
RUNNER: No it’s R12 here, there it’s R10 there because they sell pieces too

VO: Prices ranged from R10 at Croton Road, to 11 on Woodville Road and R15 at both Major Culvert Road and at the barracks close to Landsdowne Road.

INSIDER: They do tend to have meetings and try and get on the same page with regards to pricing. but the pricing has been the issue because that has caused in fighting

LINK: HEROIN CAPSULES ARE UNIQUE TO KZN. Drug kingpins have streamlined their operations to control quantities and keep track of merchandise.

MONIQUE: Durban is the hub of capsuling. it's actually a smart production move. it looks a lot more legitimate,// it's much easier to fill a capsule than it is to fill a straw.

VO: While it’s new in form, it’s not new in substance. Professor. Marks explains, that low grade heroin has been in the South African market, for at least 20, years.

MONIQUE: the amount of heroin that's been put in the capsules is much less than what was put in the straws. And so people are buying more capsules to be able to to get the same effect

VO: Capsules also build brand recognition in a fiercely competitive market - it allows dealers to reinforce control on their turf and even distinguish quality as this runner explained.

OPERATIVE: No orange?
RUNNER: They don’t have the orange mothers,
OPERATIVE: where can we get the orange
RUNNER: They say the orange is hard to get now

VO: It’s a massive market with different dealers peddling variations of the same drug comments Professor Marks.

MONIQUE: // they are an estimated // about 25000 heroin users just in Durbun itself. // And that's just heroin

VO: For most users, the true contents of the capsule remains a mystery. We asked Professor Thavi Govender to analyse the samples.

THAVI: // the main ingredient that we found was a diacetyl of morphine, which is called heroin, and then the mono acetyl morphine, which is the active ingredient.// we found significant differences between the colors. // not just in the potency, but also in the quantity of the material that's found in each cap. T3M8

VO: These samples were not in any way pure heroin, but rather a manually packaged concoction that included bulking agents explains Professor Govender.

THAVI: They're mainly being mixed with detergents because when we analyze them, we found a lot of inorganic material that that was left behind when we tried to extract the heroin from it.

VO: Historically rat poison was used as a bulking agent, but these samples were different.

THAVI: With the samples that we have analyzed now, there's no rat poison in it and and even when I look at the the users, our observations of them now is that // They're not like how they used to be, where they're getting stomach cramps and they can't walk around until they get their hit.

VO: Heroin has a sedating effect on users, elaborates Professor Marks.

MONIQUE: Drugs like heroin in particular, are used to to numb what I see as the burden of the future, which is compounded by the burden of the past. once you start using heroin, it's very, very difficult to come out of it.

VO: It is extremely addictive with a recovery rate of less than 1% according to Professor Govender.

THAVI: //It binds to your opioid receptors, // in your brain that controls the pain and gives you this euphoric effect. The effect normally the Half-Life is about 40 minutes.

VO: The effect through smoking is felt immediately and the dealers know they’ve got a captive market, once they’ve hooked users.

INSIDER: I don't think you will be able to eradicate the problem, but to downscale it, it's going to take an enormous effort.// It won't stop because as long as there's drugs, there's money to be made.

VO: Druglords even invest in their business by acquiring pharmaceutical capping machines. These images are of a machine, police confiscated in a 2020 raid in Pinetown, Durban.

THAVI: The machines are not hard to get. // the cheapest one costs something like twenty five thousand rands and it will do about three hundred and sixty caps in one shot, which would be less than a minute of work.

LINK: In WENTWORTH, DRUGS ARE AN OPEN SECRET // IT’s TOUGH FOR THE COMMUNITY – THEY FEAR THESE DRUGLORDS – AND DON’T TRUST THE POLICE.

MONIQUE: I think if there is a drug market, police are involved across the world. It's not a South African thing.

VO: Wentworth Angels director TRACEY WILLIAMS is a community activist, who does humanitarian work in the area - she says the people of Wentworth feel they have been forsaken by authorities.

TRACY: Our SAPS keeps telling us that they're going to sort this out with us in the next six months, in the next six months, we're going to have nobody left.

VO: She drove us around the area - pointing out hotspots in almost every road.

UPSOUND TRACY DRIVING
TRACY: This road as well, also a lot of shooting and craziness that’s been going on in this road.

VO: KZN Police Spokesperson, Bridagier Jay Naicker admits, Wentworth is a volatile area.

While he insists that arrests are being made, he acknowledges that in many cases bail is granted, especially in cases involving juveniles.

JAY: unfortunately, those youngsters are involved in some of the murders and other major crimes that are taking place in this area. and that’s our biggest challenge because even the community, when they see these people out, they don't understand that, you know, that they are entitled to bail. They feel that they've been failed by the system because these people are back on the streets//

VO: It’s a hard pill for the community to swallow, who are suspicious of the police.

TRACY: Police are aware of our drug lords in our community and the runners, they pay to take care of them.

VO: The so-called Wentworth gangster confirmed that the gangs are not at all phased by the cops.

MAC: Are the gangs, even afraid of the police?
GANGSTER: NOPE // They don't care. //They whole Wentworth police station is on the payroll

VO: The cop insider disagrees that everyones is on the take, but admits there are some rogue officers.

INSIDER: They fly under the radar. it's very frustrating. They're very clever in the way they do these things. But it's difficult to try and get them incarcerated .

VO: But Brigadier Naciker is firm that evidence is crucial in any of these investigations.

JAY: // when it comes to rogue police officers, // they have no place in the organization. But //, even with the drug kingpins, we need to get evidence to place them before court. The mere suspicion will not be severe enough to even police the matter on roll. And so we encouraging people to come forward. This is your community. You need to make a change.

VO: The community is fearful of the possible repercussions.

NOLENE: people are scared to talk, because they don't know if they're going to get shot and they don’t know if people are going to come target their homes, target their children.

VO: In these circumstances the police has to rely on covert operations to gather evidence. Brigadier Naicker says these projects are already in place.

JAY: //We have to go out there to our own observation. We have to do our own buys before. So so people won't necessarily see these police officers. They not from the area and they do work undercover.

VO: When we shared our undercover investigation with him, Brigadier Naicker was not surprised at how easy it was to do four buys in 45 minutes.

JAY: No, as I said, the community on a daily basis will contact us and see these things, but that's not that's insufficient.

VO: But time is running out for the community, who have run out of places to turn to.

TRACY: We’ve had enough body bags in this community for the last couple of months. We don't need any more.//. But we need our justice system to back us up.



PROMO 1 – 21 SECONDS
VO: Undercover operatives showed us how easy it is to buy heroin capsules at rock-bottom prices in the gang-ravaged Wentworth in Durban. We speak to a community struggling to cope with warring gangs, willing to kill for their drug market share.

NOLENE: people are scared to talk, because they don't know if they're going to get shot and they don’t know if people are going to come target their homes, target their children, target their family members.

PROMO 2 – 21 SECONDS
VO: It’s an all-out drug war in Wentworth, KZN as competing drug dealers take out the opposition in ruthless drive-by shootings, leaving a community crippled with drug addiction and at the mercy of violent gangs.

UPSOUND SHOOTING VIDEO

TRACY: Our SAPS keeps telling us that they're going to sort this out with us in the next six months, in the next six months, we're going to have nobody left.

PROMO 3 – 11 SECONDS

VO: Heroin capsules unique to KZN are packaged to look like pills. We visit gang-riddled Wentworth to not only show how easy it is to buy these capsules, but also what’s really inside them.

NOLENE: It happens like almost every day of the week VO: This Durban cop works drug related cases - he says what we’re seeing in Wentworth is often revenge killings. INSIDER: these guys are ruthless, they they're not trained marksmen or shooters, there’s no specific target that's aimed VO: One of the most recent innocent victims was 12 year old, Virdene Stanley. metadata.Summary: We covered the rise of codeine addiction in the Wentworth community back in 2018. Now it’s heroin capsules – package as pills, packing a deadly punch with dealers undercutting each other and taking out the opposition. Rival gangs shoot first and don’t ask questions. We delve into the driving forces and unpack the disturbing reality of life in Wentworth - a community crippled by poverty and drug addiction.

WHY HEROINE CAPSULES? Capping heroin makes for more time-efficient packaging and provides for easier and more precise dose allocation, with the capping machine ensuring that the same measure of heroin is inserted in every capsule, which makes counting of doses and distribution to dealers easier. Suppliers or wholesalers can service dealers who have different size customer bases, effectively removing layers of middlemen from the distribution pyramid. Capping machines means that fewer people are involved in heroin processing and the potential for information leaks is reduced, making production more secure. BRAND AWARENESS – EVEN WHEN IT COMES TO DRUGS Capsules may make it easier for drug kingpins to stash drugs with associates and keep track of merchandise. The colour and markings of the capsules is also significant. A host of different coloured heroin capsules with a variety of markings and logos have been seized in Durban busts. An identifiable capsule brand allows networks to build up a kind of ‘brand recognition’. This helps networks reinforce control over drug sales on their turf and become associated with the quality of the heroin –an important distinguishing quality in an expanding market characterized by fierce competition. SAPS members said that some drug lords sourced heroin from the same wholesalers at times, but increasingly they sought to differentiate themselves from rivals. METRO CAPSULES A TOP SELLER The case of the ‘Metro’ capsule – so called because the blue and white capsules matched Durban Metro Police vans – highlights the importance of product brand, quality and consistency in capturing, retaining and growing a market. ‘The addicts went wild for the blue and white cap when it first hit the streets,’ according to a SAPS officer. SAPS members said the capsules were sought after until either the producer’s quality dropped or poorer-quality copies emerged. The SAPS officer said police noticed a marked response to the quality of the heroin capsules. ‘If the users don’t get a good hit they will drop a dealer.’ TURF WAR There are so many little gangs operating with a number of runners on the streets. The area is a just a few blocks and every street is just about a different dealer’s turf. Even with our undercover we could see that the price discrepancies would fuel a turf war.
